entries.topicDescription: Unit testing, instrumented testing, and Compose UI testing on Android.

tips.title: Turbine simplifies testing Flow emissions without manual collector boilerplate
tips.content:
Testing a Flow by manually launching a collector coroutine, appending
emissions to a list, then asserting on that list after the fact is
verbose and easy to get subtly wrong around coroutine timing and test
dispatcher scheduling.

Turbine's test {} extension on a Flow gives you awaitItem(), awaitError(),
and awaitComplete() functions that suspend until the next relevant event
arrives, reading like a sequential assertion of exactly what the Flow
should emit and when — purpose-built for testing Flow-based code
correctly.

tips.title: Put most tests on the JVM and keep instrumented tests few
tips.content:
Local unit tests (src/test) run on your computer's JVM in milliseconds and don't need a device. Instrumented tests (src/androidTest) run on an emulator or phone and are slower and flakier, so keep them for what really needs Android: real database behavior, UI flows, and platform integration.

The way to have many fast tests is to keep logic in plain Kotlin classes (use cases, ViewModels, mappers) that don't touch Android APIs directly, and to inject anything that does.

tips.title: Replace Dispatchers.Main in ViewModel tests
tips.content:
Code that uses viewModelScope launches on Dispatchers.Main, which doesn't exist in a plain JVM test and throws. Swap it for a test dispatcher before each test and reset it afterwards. A small JUnit rule keeps that out of every test class.

Then wrap the test body in runTest, so delays are skipped and coroutines complete deterministically.

tips.title: Test Compose UI through semantics, not through view IDs
tips.content:
Compose has no views to find by ID. UI tests use the semantics tree: createComposeRule hosts your composable, onNode finders locate nodes by text, content description or a testTag, and actions and assertions run on them. The rule waits for the UI to be idle before each step, so you rarely need sleeps.

Prefer finding by visible text or accessibility description, which also verifies accessibility, and use testTag for elements that have neither.

tips.title: Prefer fakes over mocks for your own repositories
tips.content:
A mock verifies that specific calls happened, which couples the test to how the code works internally: refactor without changing behavior and the test breaks. A fake is a small working implementation (an in-memory repository) that the test drives through its public behavior and then asserts on results.

Fakes are reusable across tests, read like real code, and work naturally with Flow. Keep mocks for boundaries you can't fake easily or where the interaction itself is the behavior.
